Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Kofi had always been drawn to a career in law enforcement, hoping to make a difference in his community. As an 18-year-old police officer, he took pride in his work, patrolling the streets of his hometown with a sense of purpose. However, Kofi's confidence was not as unwavering as it seemed. Behind the badge and uniform, he harbored a deep-seated fear that had been festering since childhood. Growing up, Kofi had witnessed the horrors of domestic violence in his own home. He remembered the sound of shattering glass, the thud of fists on flesh, and the terror-stricken faces of his loved ones. The memories were etched in his mind like snapshots, each one a vivid picture of a moment that felt frozen in time. Whenever these memories resurfaced, Kofi's body would involuntarily contort into the same defensive position he had assumed as a child, as if bracing himself for impact. As a police officer, Kofi found himself on high alert whenever he encountered unfamiliar situations or people acting suspiciously. His eyes would scan the environment for potential threats, and he couldn't help but notice objects that could be used as weapons – a broken bottle on the ground, a sharp edge on a nearby surface. The silence of an empty alleyway or a quiet room would send his heart racing, making him feel like something was about to go terribly wrong. Kofi had come to believe that he couldn't rely on himself, that his reactions since the event meant he was losing his grip on reality. He felt helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to those around him or even to himself. The weight of these fears made him avoid going to unfamiliar places, where he couldn't assess the danger lurking in every corner. Physical touch had also become a source of discomfort for Kofi. Being touched unprepared would send him recoiling, as if his body was anticipating an attack. He had learned to be constantly on guard, never letting his defenses down, not even around those closest to him. As time passed, Kofi's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on his relationships and daily life. His colleagues noticed that he seemed distant, always scanning the surroundings instead of engaging with them during downtime. His friends and family grew concerned about his increasing isolation, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking on thin ice. The final straw came when Kofi responded to a domestic violence call, only to find himself frozen in the same defensive position as he had been all those years ago. The flashback that followed left him shaken and doubting his ability to perform his duties as an officer. For the first time, Kofi realized that he needed help to confront the demons of his past. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kofi's eyes darted around the room, still searching for potential threats. He was scared, but more than anything, he hoped that with treatment, he could learn to trust himself again and find a way to quiet the constant whispers of fear that had haunted him for so long.
